newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE HOLDS FIRST ROUND LEAD AT U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE HOLDS FIRST ROUND LEAD AT U.S. OPEN.

text.p: Colin Montgomerie, who had said that Congresssional Country Club's treacherous golf course suited his game, proved it Thursday by shooting a five-under-par 65 to lead the first round of the U.S. Open.

Montgomerie, who says he loves tough courses, made Congressional -- the longest course in Open history -- look anything but tough as he birdied five of seven holes in the middle of his near-flawless round.

Hal Sutton, winner of the 1983 PGA Championship, and Steve Stricker -- both of whom have struggled on the tour this year -- shot four-under par 66s to stand second to Montgomerie, whose 65 matched his best effort in 22 U.S. Open rounds.

British Open champion Tom Lehman, who tied for second last year, and Mark McNulty of Zimbabwe both posted 67s for third place. They were one ahead of Hideki Kase of Japan, a rookie on the U.S. PGA Tour, and Nike Tour player Dave Schreyer -- who were both making their U.S. Open debuts.
Jeff Sluman, another former PGA champion who was second in the 1992 Open, was tied at 69 with Justin leonard, who won last week's Kemper Open just down the road.

Montgomerie said accuracy off the tee -- his speciality -- was the key to his fine round on a 7,213-yard course, where many top players struggled amid the thick rough, deep bunkers and four dangerous water holes.
"I love this form of golf, where hitting fairways means something and par means something," Montgomerie said after getting off to his best start by far in this championship.
"You can't play this golf course from the rough," added Montgomerie, who hit 13 of 14 fairways -- using a 3-wood.

On the only hole where Montgomerie missed the fairway, the very difficult sixth -- a par-5 turned into a 475-yard par-4 -- he managed to save par when he hit his 8-iron third shot stiff after driving into deep rough.
"That was the most vital hole of the day," Montgomerie said. "It was the most important par I've made in a long time."

Montgomerie, who has an excellent record in U.S. Opens, including a second and a third-place finish, could have been a stroke better, but he bogeyed the 480-yard, par-4 17th for the only blemish on his scorecard.
Tiger Woods, the young Masters champion and a heavy favourite here, got off to a rocky start and played very inconsistently throughout the warm, cloudy day.

He began par, birdie, bogey, birdie, bogey, par, birdie and made the turn at one under. However, after a birdie at the 10th, he made a double bogey at the 11th, bogeys at 13 and 15 and a double bogey at the par-3 last, where he dunked his tee shot in the lake shared by the 17th and 18th holes.
After finishing at four-over 74, the 21-year-old three-time U.S. Amateur champion stalked off the 18th green and headed right to the parking lot without talking to reporters.
He later told a championship official that he simply hit too many bad shots, especially on the back nine.

Asked what he was thinking after his disappointing round, a subdued Woods said: "I don't know." Asked what he was going to do, he again answered: "I don't know," according to a transcript of the conversation.
Montgomerie opened with six pars and then birdied the seventh and ninth holes, sinking three-footers on each, to make the turn at two-under-par 33.

He then birdied numbers 10, 12, 13 and 16 -- all from 15 feet or less -- to go to six under. But he gave one back at the 17th, Congressional's signature hole, a long, downhill par-4 whose green is nestled on the lake shore across from the 18th green.

Montgomerie, the best player on the European PGA Tour for the past four years, put his approach in a bunker to the right of the green, blasted to about 15 feet but then missed the putt as his ball just slipped past the hole.
He then made a routine par at the 190-yard 18th -- the first par-3 to conclude a U.S. Open since 1909 -- despite the presence of a big, black snake just off the green.

"Those things happen. It came out of the water, I believe," Montgomerie said. "The crowd seemed more intent on watching the snake than (watching) me trying to putt for 64, which was fine. It took the pressure off."
Montgomerie, however, missed the birdie try for 64.
Still, Montgomerie -- who says this is the championship he most wants to win -- was delighted with his round, which he called "about the best round I ever put together."
Despite his lead, however, Montgomerie knew there was still a lot of golf yet to be played.
"I've only done seven of the 28 miles (45 km)," he said, referring to four trips over Congressional's 7,213 yards.
"There's an awful long way to go, but I'm in position where I can compete."
